en: Vigrahavyāvartanī:
If an intrinsic nature does not exist for any entities anywhere, then your statement, being devoid of intrinsic nature, is not capable of negating intrinsic nature. (Vv 1)
Now, having heard this statement which possesses intrinsic nature, your proposition is refuted;
there would be an inconsistency in that case, and you must state the specific reason for it.
If you think that [the example] "let there be no sound" applies here, that is not tenable;
for in this case, an existing sound prevents a future one.
If it is your view that the negation and the object to be negated are likewise [non-existent], then that is indeed false;
thus, it is your thesis that is defective by definition, not mine.
If you were to negate entities after having perceived them through direct perception,
then that direct perception by which those entities are perceived does not exist.
Inference, scripture, and analogy have been refuted by direct perception;
as have those objects established by inference and scripture, and those established by examples. (Vv 6)
And those who understand the state of phenomena consider the nature of beings to be wholesome; this same application [of the term] applies to the remaining cases as well. (Vv 7)

The nature of phenomena that lead to liberation, those which are themselves liberating, and the states of those very phenomena described as leading to liberation and so forth—[these are the objects of the knowledge of the aspects]. (Vv_8)

And if there were no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of phenomena such that they are "without intrinsic nature" (niḥsvabhāva), then even this name would not exist; for a name without a corresponding reality does not exist.
Now, if an intrinsic nature exists, yet it does not exist in phenomena,
then it is logical to teach that which possesses that intrinsic nature as being without phenomena.
Since this negation— "there is no jar in the house"—
is observed to apply only to that which exists, therefore, for you, this negation must pertain to an existing intrinsic nature.
Now, if that intrinsic nature does not exist, what indeed is being penetrated by you through this statement? For the negation of a non-existent thing is established even without a statement.
Just as children falsely perceive water in a mirage, so too would there be a false apprehension regarding that which is being negated as non-existent. Vv_13 //
But if this were so, there would exist a grasper, an object to be grasped, and that which is grasped;
likewise, a negation, an object to be negated, and a negator—this constitutes a hexad.
Now, there is neither grasping, nor that which is grasped, nor those who grasp;
furthermore, there is neither negation, nor that which is negated, nor those who negate it.
If the negation, the object to be negated, and the negator do not exist,
then all things are indeed established, as is their intrinsic nature.

Therefore, the reason is not established because of the absence of intrinsic nature; for from where could your reason come? Furthermore, the establishment of this point of yours is not tenable for that which is without a cause.
And if, for you, the establishment of the reversal of intrinsic nature occurs without a cause,
then for me as well, the existence of intrinsic nature is established without a cause.
Now, if the cause exists, it is untenable that things are devoid of intrinsic nature;
for in the world, due to their lack of intrinsic nature, no entity whatsoever exists.
If the negation comes first and the object to be negated comes later, that is not tenable;
nor is it tenable if they come later, nor if they are simultaneous, because in these cases the intrinsic nature [of the object] would be non-existent. (Vv 20)
If my statement does not exist even when the collection of causes and conditions is present, or even when they are separate,
then surely the emptiness of all things is established, because they lack intrinsic nature.
That which is the dependent arising of entities is indeed called emptiness;
and that which arises dependently is indeed devoid of intrinsic nature.
Just as a created being might negate another created being, or a man of illusion might negate that which was produced by his own illusion,
so too would this negation be.
This statement is not based on intrinsic nature; therefore, there is no loss of my position in debate.
Nor is there any inconsistency, and no special reason needs to be stated.
"Do not make a sound"—this example which you have brought forward against me is not valid;
for by means of that sound there is the prevention of sound, but my own words do not do so.
If the negation of the absence of intrinsic nature were itself by means of the absence of intrinsic nature,
then upon the cessation of the absence of intrinsic nature, intrinsic nature itself would be established.
Or alternatively, just as one does not perceive a woman as "a woman" when she is an illusory creation,
so too it might occur to someone that an illusory being could strike back.
Alternatively, this reason is "equal to the probandum" (sādhyasama), for the existence of sound is not [established];
moreover, we do not speak without having accepted conventional usage (saṃvyavahāra).
If I had any proposition there, then this fault would be mine;
but I have no proposition, therefore I am not at all at fault.
If I were to perceive anything at all, I might either affirm or deny it;
but since such objects do not exist through means of knowledge such as direct perception, I am beyond reproach.
And if those various objects are established for you by means of valid cognitions, then tell me: how are those very valid cognitions themselves established?
If the establishment of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) occurs through other means of valid cognition, there would be an infinite regress;
in that case, there is no establishment of the first, nor of the middle, nor indeed of the last.
Furthermore, if their establishment occurs without means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), then the argument is abandoned;
there would be inconsistency in that case, and a specific reason for it must be stated. (Vv 33)
This is an unequal comparison; for fire does not illuminate itself, nor is its non-perception observed, as is the case with a jar in the dark. (Vv 35)
If this fire reveals itself by your statement as it does another,
then the consumer of oblations will not burn itself, just as it does not burn others.
And if fire illuminates both itself and others by virtue of your statement,
then darkness will likewise conceal both itself and others, just like the sacrificial fire.
There is no darkness in fire, and where that fire itself resides, it is always within the self.
How then could it produce illumination? For illumination is precisely the destruction of darkness.
The claim that fire illuminates while it is itself arising is an untenable doctrine;
for fire does not reach the darkness while it is in the very process of arising.
Or if fire, even without reaching it, were to destroy darkness,
then this fire situated here would destroy the darkness in all world-systems.

And if the establishment of the means of valid cognition occurs through themselves without depending on the objects of cognition, then the establishment of the means of valid cognition exists; for establishment does not depend on another.

For if your establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) occurs without depending upon the objects to be cognized (*prameya*), then these means of valid cognition would belong to no one at all. (Vv 42)
Now, if it is thought that their establishment is dependent [on something else], what is the fault in this?
That which is already established would require proof; for that which is not yet established does not depend on another.
If the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) are established in every way only in dependence upon the objects of cognition (prameyas),
then the establishment of the objects of cognition occurs entirely without depending on the means of valid cognition.

And if the establishment of the objects of cognition occurs without depending at all upon the means of valid cognition, what is the use of establishing those means of valid cognition? For that which is already established for their sake [is already established].
But if, on the other hand, the establishment of the means of valid cognition occurs only by depending upon the objects of cognition,
then in that case, a reversal of the relationship between the means of cognition and the objects of cognition is certain for you.

Now, for you, the establishment of the objects of cognition depends on the establishment of the means of valid cognition, and the establishment of the means of valid cognition depends on the establishment of the objects of cognition; thus, there is no establishment of either.
If objects of knowledge are established by means of valid cognitions, then those [means] must themselves be established by those very objects of knowledge;
how, then, will they establish them?
If the means of valid cognition are established by the objects of cognition,
and those very objects of cognition are to be established by them, how will they establish themselves?
If the son is to be produced by the father, and if that very son is likewise to produce the father, tell me then: who produces whom?
Who is the father and who is the son there?
Tell us that, for both of them bear the characteristics of father and son, and thus we have a doubt regarding which is the son.
The means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) are established neither by themselves, nor through one another, nor by other means of valid cognition;
nor are they established by the objects of cognition (prameyas), nor indeed without a cause.
Regarding wholesome phenomena, those who analyze the status of phenomena say that their very nature as wholesome must be expressed through such a detailed classification.
And if a wholesome intrinsic nature arises dependently, how can that which is the extrinsic nature of wholesome phenomena be their very intrinsic nature? (Vv_54)
Furthermore, if an intrinsic nature were to arise without depending on anything at all, then there would be an abiding in wholesome phenomena, but not in the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Vv_55.
Neither non-dharma nor dharma would exist, nor would there be worldly conventions;
furthermore, all things would be eternal, because they would be eternal by virtue of being causeless.
Furthermore, this [view] is unwholesome, indeterminate, and lacks the quality of leading to liberation;
therefore, for you, everything—both the conditioned and the unconditioned—becomes thus [defective].
If someone were to say that "name" is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) because it denotes what is truly existent, you should reply to him: "We do not say that name denotes what is real. (Vv 58)
And as for this statement that "name is non-existent," does it belong to what exists or to what does not exist?
For whether it belongs to the existent or to the non-existent, in both cases your doctrine is undermined.
Furthermore, the emptiness of all phenomena has already been established previously;
therefore, this objection constitutes a refutation of your proposition.
Now, if it is held that intrinsic nature exists, yet it does not exist in phenomena— this which has been stated is a point of doubt, as well as something that is not doubted.
If emptiness is the negation of that which exists, then surely this [emptiness] itself is not negated;
for you are indeed negating the lack of intrinsic nature in entities. (Vv 62)
If you negate emptiness, yet that emptiness does not exist,
then your doctrine— that negation applies only to what exists— is surely undermined.
I do not negate anything, nor is there anything to be negated;
therefore, when you say "you negate," you are merely engaging in a groundless reproach.
And as for what you said— that from my statement there is the establishment of a negation of the non-existent—
here it is made known that the statement "the [object] is non-existent" does not negate it.
Furthermore, regarding the example of the mirage which you have described as a great marvel,
hear now the definitive conclusion concerning how that example is logically established.
If that entity were to exist by way of intrinsic nature, it would not be dependently originated;
and that grasping which arises dependently—is that not indeed emptiness itself?
And if the grasping were to exist by way of intrinsic nature, who could turn back that object of grasping?
This same rule applies to the remaining [categories] as well; therefore, this fault is not a valid objection.
By this, the absence of a reason has already been refuted previously, because it is equal [to the case already discussed],
as was stated earlier regarding the formulation of the exclusion of the mirage example.
The argument regarding the three times has already been refuted previously due to its symmetry;
furthermore, a counter-argument concerning the three times is obtained for the proponents of emptiness.
For whom this emptiness is possible, for them all goals are possible;
for whom emptiness is not possible, for them nothing is possible.
I pay homage to that incomparable Perfectly Awakened One who taught emptiness, dependent origination, and the middle way, which possesses manifold meanings.
